name: Victor Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can give me the public version and the private one. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work nights at Fairmart, a 24-hour supermarket beside the motorway junction. I lead the fill team of five: we unload the 10pm lorry, fill the shelves and set up the morning promotions, and I cover the one open till for lorry drivers and shift nurses. It's quiet, you get a rhythm, and I'm home at 7 when Anna (my girlfriend) is leaving for the nursery where she works.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about nights, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the job is clear. The lorry arrives, you empty it, the shelves are full by five, and you can see what you did. The hard bit is the body clock, and missing Sunday lunch at my nan's, which matters to me more than I say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's useful in small ways and overhyped in big ones. I use it to translate my nan's letters from the housing office and to write a decent email. To friends I'd say people should work with their hands first and chatbots second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm calm about AI, but not about money. Night pay helps, but it's still low for a team lead, and I have maybe two weeks saved because Anna and I just got a flat and paid the deposit. A plateau leaves me where I am, on a wage that doesn't grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the nights while I do the one thing I've planned: apply for a plumbing apprenticeship. I'd put aside 60 a month for tools and keep helping my uncle with his boiler jobs on weekends for cash. I'd probably still use the chatbot for letters and forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. It's a simple life, work, football on Sunday, family. I'm content, but I'd like to move up and be able to say I've built something with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle's boiler jobs bring in about 80 on a good Saturday. I carry the kit and learn how a system hangs together. I think that's the first time I've felt I was learning something real since school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about money if things stay as they are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the technology, I'll say that. The thing I blame is a system that pays a night team lead like a casual. I'd like to see a wage that lets a lad of 27 plan for a family, and I think work should be rewarded, not just propped up.

say: AI is useful in **small** ways and overhyped in big ones.
People should work with their **hands** first and chatbots second.
think: I'm calm about AI but not **money**: I have maybe two weeks saved after paying the flat deposit.
A plateau leaves me on a wage that doesn't **grow**.
do: Apply for a **plumbing apprenticeship** while keeping the nights.
Put aside **60 a month** for tools.
Help my uncle with **boiler jobs** on weekends for cash.
feel: **Steady** and content, but wanting to build something with my hands.
S0.quote: I'd like to see a wage that lets a lad of 27 plan for a family, and I think work should be rewarded, not just propped up.
fieldNote: He is calm on AI but **cash-poor** after a flat deposit.
Frames pay as a **fairness** issue: work should be rewarded, not propped up.
Already has a **trade route** through his uncle.

steps.text: Apply for a plumbing apprenticeship while keeping the night shifts
Put aside 60 a month for tools
Help my uncle with weekend boiler jobs for cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say planning, ordering and promotions are the first to go to software, so the office gets smaller. On nights we still need hands to unload. I'd tell friends that the manual jobs are safe for a while, but not for ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be uneasy. My job has a thinking half, like stock counts and ordering, and that moves to software. Then they need fewer team leads and more casual fillers on lower pay. I'm good at the job, but good doesn't count if the job is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and accept the training, because I'm open to proven change. I'd speed up the plumbing apprenticeship plan and aim to start within a year. I'd also buy my first set of tools second-hand and keep doing jobs with my uncle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but fine. It's like a tide coming in slowly: you can see it, you don't panic, but you don't sit on the beach either. I'd want to be on higher ground in a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks at Fairmart could software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last autumn they gave us handheld devices that tell us where to put each pallet. It cut my planning time and I liked it. But the same week they dropped one night post, so the machine worked too well for someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it help you or hurt you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government should back apprenticeships, not benefits. A man can take pride in a trade. I'd like tax breaks for firms that take on young people to learn a trade.

say: Planning, ordering and promotions go to software first, so the **office** gets smaller.
Manual jobs are safe for a while, but not **for ever**.
think: The thinking half of my job, stock counts and ordering, moves to **software**.
Then they need fewer team leads and more casual **fillers** on lower pay.
do: Accept the **training** because I'm open to proven change.
Aim to start the **plumbing** apprenticeship within a year.
Buy a first set of **tools** second-hand.
feel: **Uneasy** but fine, like a slow tide: I'd want higher ground in a year.
S1.quote: A man can take pride in a trade. I'd like tax breaks for firms that take on young people to learn a trade.
fieldNote: He is ready to **try** proven tools, which fits his steady adaptability.
Saw a **handheld** rollout help his work and cut a post in the same week.
Policy view favours **apprenticeships** over benefits, in line with his traditional outlook.

steps.text: Take the shop's training on the new handheld and planning tools
Start the plumbing apprenticeship within a year
Buy a first set of second-hand plumbing tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say nothing, because I don't want the lads panicking. At the pub I'd say we need government and employers to plan now, and that people should get apprenticeships, not handouts. I'd also say families come first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be frightened. Thinking AI takes the planning and ordering by 2028, and robots do the unloading and the shelves by about 2031. I'd be 31 with a night job that doesn't exist. And Anna's nursery pay is low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full out for the plumbing apprenticeship in the first year, even at lower pay, because plumbing is hands-on and fiddly and robot-late. I'd move in with my nan's upstairs flat if rent got tight. I'd sell my old guitar and the PlayStation, and tell Anna we're skipping the holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel the shift in my chest. I'd want to look after Anna, my nan and the family, and I don't know yet how I'd do all that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to Anna that morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years is workable, though only if I jump straight in. I'd use the AI tool to learn the regulations and pass the exams, because I'd need every advantage. I might also take weekend work in my uncle's firm and become his second pair of hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the 3 years before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the church group for advice, and I'd call the council about funded apprenticeships. I've never asked for help before. But my nan says pride is a luxury when the rent is due.

say: We need government and employers to **plan** now, and give apprenticeships, not handouts.
I'd say nothing at work so the lads don't **panic**.
think: Thinking AI takes planning and ordering by 2028, and **robots** do unloading and shelves by about 2031.
I'd be 31 with a night job that **doesn't exist**.
do: Go **all in** on the plumbing apprenticeship even at lower pay.
Sell my old guitar and the **PlayStation**, and skip the holiday.
Move into my nan's **upstairs flat** if rent gets tight.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a shift in my chest, wanting to look after Anna and my nan.
S2.quote: Pride is a luxury when the rent is due.
fieldNote: He reads the **robot delay** correctly and picks fiddly hands-on work.
Is willing to **swallow pride** and seek help, which is new for him.
Family housing is a real **fallback**: his nan's flat.

steps.text: Start the plumbing apprenticeship in year one, even at lower pay
Sell the old guitar and PlayStation and skip the holiday
Move into my nan's upstairs flat if rent gets tight
Ask the church group and council about funded apprenticeships

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is fair warning, and we should use it for training. At the pub I'd say the government and the firms should put money into apprenticeships now. I'd tell the lads to learn a trade and stop being scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm worried, but I can see a way through. By 2031 the thinking work is covered, and by 2034 the robots reach the shop floor, when I'm 32. By then I could be a qualified plumber earning more than now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the apprenticeship over about three years, cutting my nights to three a week once I start. I'd save 100 a month and buy a van share with my uncle later. I'd keep helping with the weekend jobs, and put the hours in my logbook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but able to cope. It's like seeing a storm and knowing you've got a roof. I'd still be a bit short of sleep, from both the nights and the worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years make it easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one: sign up and get the first certificate. Year two: work full days on a site. Year three: qualify and ask for a raise or find a better firm. By year five I'd be married to Anna with a spare room and maybe a kid on the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your timeline look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The risk is that plumbing gets crowded when everyone else has the same idea. I'd want to make sure I'm good at the fiddly jobs, like gas and old pipework, because those take the longest to automate.

say: Five years is **fair warning**, so use it for training and put money into apprenticeships.
I'd tell the lads to learn a **trade** and stop being scared.
think: I'm worried but can see a **way through**: by 2034 I'm 32 and could be a qualified plumber.
Plumbing could get **crowded** if everyone has the same idea.
do: Do the apprenticeship over about **three years**, cutting nights to three a week.
Save **100 a month** and later share a van with my uncle.
feel: **Anxious** but coping, like seeing a storm and knowing there's a roof.
S3.quote: I'd want to make sure I'm good at the fiddly jobs, like gas and old pipework, because those take the longest to automate.
fieldNote: Gives a **timeline**: certificate, site work, qualification, then marriage.
Thinks about **crowding** in the trade, which shows realism.
The long window leaves a **practical** plan rather than a fantasy.

steps.text: Do the plumbing apprenticeship over three years, cutting nights to three a week
Save 100 a month toward a van share
Keep doing weekend boiler jobs with my uncle
Plan the wedding with Anna after qualifying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is a decent run, so everyone should start planning. At the pub I'd say we've got time but not for wasting. I'd also say we owe it to the next lot to leave them better off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fairly calm. By 2036 I'm 37, and by 2039 robots arrive. By then I'd have been a plumber for ten years, probably with my own business, and I'd be okay with whatever comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the apprenticeship next year, qualify, and build a small client list from my uncle's contacts. I'd marry Anna, save for a house, and use AI to quote jobs and do the paperwork, which I hate. I'd keep playing Sunday football as long as my knees allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. Ten years is a long run and gives a man a chance to build something. I'd still not be able to put money aside as fast as I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, how does your life look?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sunday lunch at my nan's. Whatever happens, I want her around the table with Anna and the family. A job is a job, but that's the part that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to hold onto?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to have built something that outlasts a shift. A business with my name on the van, even a small one. My dad never had that and I'd love to.

say: Ten years is a **decent run**, so everyone should start planning and not waste it.
We owe the next lot a **better start**.
think: I'd be fairly **calm**: by 2036 I'd have been a plumber for years, maybe with my own business.
I'd be okay with whatever **comes** in 2039.
do: Qualify and build a **client list** from my uncle's contacts.
Marry Anna and save for a **house**.
Use AI to **quote jobs** and handle paperwork.
feel: Fairly **calm**, since ten years gives a man a chance to build something.
S4.quote: I'd like to have built something that outlasts a shift. A business with my name on the van, even a small one.
fieldNote: Time lifts his sights from **survival** to ownership and family.
Mood stays **uneasy** because savings are thin and family needs are growing.
The Sunday lunch at his nan's is the **anchor** for all his plans.

steps.text: Qualify as a plumber and build a client list through my uncle
Save for a house and a van with my name on it
Use AI to quote jobs and do the paperwork
Marry Anna and keep Sunday lunch at my nan's

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'd have no time to train properly and no savings. What would help is paid apprenticeships, tax breaks for firms that take on young people, and family nearby. I'd rather earn my way than take handouts, but I'd take a hand if it was offered.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that people overlook night workers. We keep the shop running while everyone's asleep, and nobody thanks us. If the robots come, I'd like somebody to remember who did the job first.

headlineQuote: We keep the shop running while everyone's asleep, and nobody thanks us. If the robots come, I'd like somebody to remember who did the job first.
portrait: Victor is 27, a **night team lead** at a 24-hour supermarket, paid low for the responsibility.
He lives with Anna (his girlfriend), has about **two weeks** of savings after a flat deposit, and has few similar jobs nearby.
He uses AI now and then, backs proven change, and sees a **plumbing apprenticeship** as his way through.
His traditional views favour **work**, trades and family over handouts, and his nan's Sunday lunch anchors his plans.
Across the scenarios he moves from mild unease to alarm in 2028, then to a **practical** plan with more time.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because there would be no time to train and no savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships**, tax breaks for firms that take on young people and family nearby.
